Grade 1 · Unit 1-B

Parts, Parents, and Young

How do outside parts, parents, and young help living things survive?

Living things have parts that do jobs, and young animals and plants grow up to look like their parents, but not exactly. In this unit you will connect beaks, feet, roots and leaves to what they help a living thing do, see how people copy nature's designs, and look at how some animal parents care for their young.

In this lesson

  1. External parts help survival
  2. Biomimicry design
  3. Parent-offspring behavior
  4. Young are like, but not exactly like, parents
  5. Try it at home
  6. Check yourself
  7. Play: Part Match Safari

You did this before / what is new. This is new in grade 1: matching body parts to jobs, copying a part to solve a problem, parent-offspring behavior patterns, and a same/different trait tally.

Concept 1

External parts help survival

Outside parts (external parts) such as beaks, feet, roots, stems, and leaves help living things get food, move, and stay safe.

Diagram

Beaver, deer, and sugar maple leaf with parts labeled.

“A beaver’s flat tail helps it steer and balance when it swims.”

Try it

Match beak, foot, or root cards to their jobs.

  • Beak: hummingbird’s long thin beak (sips nectar from flowers)
  • Beak: cardinal’s thick cone beak (cracks seeds)
  • Beak: duck’s flat bill (sifts food out of water)
  • Beak: hawk’s hooked beak (tears meat)
  • Foot: duck’s webbed feet (swim)
  • Foot: woodpecker’s clawed feet (grip tree bark)
  • Root: holds the plant in the soil and takes in water

Job cards:

  • sips nectar
  • cracks seeds
  • sifts food from water
  • tears meat
  • swim
  • grip tree bark
  • hold the plant and take in water

Which beak picks seeds? The cardinal’s thick cone beak.

“Which beak picks seeds?”

Real world

White-tailed deer in Michigan woods have ears that help them hear danger.

“Big ears help deer listen.”

Data

Class chart: each part and its job.

“Webbed feet: swim.”

Concept 2

Biomimicry design

Biomimicry means copying the shape or job of a plant or animal part to solve a problem people have.

Analogy

A burr is like a hook-and-loop strap (a strap with hooks on one side and loops on the other). Burr’s tiny hooks = the hooks on the strap (= means “is the same as”). Fur or a sock = the loops the hooks grab. People copied the burr’s hooks to make the strap.

“A burr grabs. We can copy it.”

Try it

Guess first: Which part of a plant or animal could help you solve a problem? Pick one.

What you need:

  • picture cards
  • paper
  • tape
  • fabric scraps
  • cotton balls
  • paper clips
  • pipe cleaners
  • a small tray

Do: Choose a problem (pick one):

  • stay dry
  • carry seeds
  • stay warm

Pick a part to copy:

  • a leaf (stays dry)
  • fur (stays warm)
  • a burr (grabs)

Build a model helper. Test it: sprinkle water, hold it on your hand, or try to pick up paper “seeds”.

Look for: Did the helper work? What part of nature did it copy? What would you change?

What it shows: People get ideas from nature’s parts. This is called biomimicry.

Safety: Small pieces need an adult close by. Do not use live wild animals.

“I copied a part from nature. I tested it.”

Data

Test table: “Did it help?”

“My burr hook picked up paper seeds.”

Real world

Burrs gave a people problem an answer. Many years ago, a Swiss engineer named George de Mestral came home from a walk with burrs stuck to his pants and to his dog’s fur. He looked at a burr up close and saw its tiny hooks. He copied the hooks to make a strap with hooks on one side and loops on the other. That strap is called a hook-and-loop fastener. You may find one on shoes, jackets, or backpacks.

Look for burrs on a walk near you, in a field or along a trail in Michigan.

“Nature gives ideas.”

Concept 3

Parent-offspring behavior

Some animal parents feed, protect, or guide their young (baby animals). Parent-offspring behavior means what a parent does to help its young. We look at examples and ask what the parent does and how it helps the young survive. Not every animal has this care.

Analogy

Parent care is like a helper blanket. The blanket = what the parent does (feeds, guards, guides). The one under the blanket = the baby animal. A blanket keeps you warm and safe, and care keeps young animals safe.

Where it breaks: not every animal parent cares for its young.

“Care keeps young safe.”

Try it

Read-aloud text, short video, or picture cards:

  • robin feeding chicks
  • ducklings following their mother
  • deer hiding fawns

“What does the parent do?”

Data

A pattern is something that happens again and again.

Pattern chart: the parent, what it does, and how it helps the young.

“Robin feeds. Mother duck leads. Mother deer hides her fawn.”

Real world

Michigan robins feed chicks in spring.

“Robins feed their chicks.”

Concept 4

Young are like, but not exactly like, parents

Young plants and animals look like their parents, but they are not exactly the same.

Try it

Match each adult with its young:

  • deer and fawn
  • robin and chick
  • maple tree and seedling

“Fawns look like deer, but smaller.”

Data

A trait is something we can see, like color, shape, or spots. Tally the traits that are the same and the traits that are different.

“Both have four legs. Spots are different. A fawn’s spots fade as it grows up.”

Diagram

Adult and young side by side with arrows showing “like” and “different.”

“Like, but not exactly like.”

Real world

A seedling is a baby plant that grew from a seed. A sugar maple seedling looks like a small sugar maple tree.

“A tiny maple looks like a maple.”

Hands-on · Design or investigate

Try it at home or in class

Biomimicry Helper Challenge. Problem: a person needs help staying dry, carrying small seeds, or keeping warm. Students choose a natural external part to mimic, such as a leaf, fur, shell, or burr. They build a model helper, test it, and record whether it worked. Criteria: the helper works in a simple test and the student can name the natural part copied. Constraints: use only kit materials.

Try it

What you need

  • Michigan plant and animal picture cards
  • paper
  • tape
  • fabric scraps
  • cotton balls
  • paper clips
  • pipe cleaners
  • crayons
  • magnifier
  • small tray

Optional: bean seeds and cups if comparing plant young and adults.

Safety: Small parts need supervision. If using soil, seeds, or outdoor plants, wash hands after the activity. Do not use live wild animals.

Try it

What you do

1. Parts and jobs (10 minutes). Play the match game above. Make a class chart: part and job.

2. Biomimicry helper (25 minutes). Pick a problem and a natural part, build a helper, test it, and record whether it worked.

3. Parent care (10 minutes). Listen to a read-aloud or look at picture cards. Fill in: parent, action, how it helps the young.

4. Alike and different (10 minutes). Look at adult and young pairs. List what is alike and what is different.

Words to know

external part
an outside body part or plant part.
survive
stay alive and grow.
beak
mouth part birds use.
root
plant part that takes in water.
leaf
plant part that helps use sunlight.
behavior
something a living thing does.
offspring
young living thing.
trait
something we can observe, like color or shape.
mimic
copy in a useful way.
biomimicry
solving a human problem by copying nature.
Tutor notes: misconceptions, pacing

Pacing: 5 sessions of 30 minutes.

Common misconceptions to listen for:

  • “Baby animals are exactly like their parents.” Correct: young are very much like, but not exactly like, their parents.
  • “Young animals do not need parents.” Correct: many parents feed, protect, and teach young; care helps survival.
  • “Only body parts help; behaviors do not help.” Correct: behaviors such as feeding and protecting also help survival.
  • “Biomimicry means copying a whole animal exactly.” Correct: we copy a useful shape, pattern, or job.
  • “Living things cannot help solve human problems.” Correct: plant and animal parts can inspire useful designs.
  • “External parts are only for looking nice.” Correct: external parts have jobs.
  • “Young are not like parents at all.” Correct: young often resemble parents in many observable ways.

Limits and cautions:

  • Parent care varies across animals; teach these as patterns, not rules for every species.
  • Avoid saying all baby animals are cute or helpless; some are independent quickly.
  • Biomimicry models must stay simple; a good test matters more than a fancy build.
  • This unit does not teach cells, genes, or inherited trait mechanisms. Those belong in later grades.
  • Simplification: “parents help young” is a grade-1 pattern; real animal behavior is more varied.

Connections: - Builds on: K2.0 Science Noticing and Asking *(optional)*, K-C Living Things and Their Homes for needs and habitats. - Builds toward: Unit 7: Cells, Unit 8: Classifying Life, Unit 9: Body Systems & Homeostasis, Unit 12: Ecosystems & Food Webs.
